session_meta.research_objective:
Focus group guide exploring how men in the UK make everyday food
choices, how social context, work, hobbies, health, taste and other
people shape what they eat, how gender and masculinity may influence
food choices, and what would need to change for plant-based foods to
become more acceptable or appealing.
session_meta.topic_domain: Masculinity, food choice, animal product consumption, and plant-based eating
session_meta.participant_collective_identity: Men in the UK reflecting on food choices, male friendship, gender norms, and plant-based eating
session_meta.moderator_knowledge_brief:
Explore (1) everyday food decision-making, (2) the social contexts in
which men spend time with male friends, (3) the influence of other
people, work, hobbies, health, nutrition and taste on food choices,
(4) whether participants perceive gender as shaping what they eat,
(5) social acceptability and gendered meanings attached to vegetarian,
vegan, plant-based, feminine or masculine foods, and (6) what personal,
social and practical changes would make plant-based eating more viable
or appealing. The discussion should remain exploratory, non-judgmental,
and non-leading.

initial_session_plan.thematisation_approach: I will frame participants as men going about ordinary everyday life — making food choices, spending time with friends, navigating work and leisure — rather than as research subjects reflecting on masculinity or gender. The collective identity is grounded in the mundane and specific: what they actually eat, where they actually go, who they actually spend time with. This keeps the entry point concrete and socially comfortable before the discussion moves into more sensitive territory.
priority_research_areas: Gender and food choice (Section 3): Highest social desirability risk — men may deny that gender influences their choices or retreat to purely pragmatic explanations. Will require behavioural grounding ('can you think of a time when...') and readiness to surface contradictions between stated attitudes and described behaviours.

Imagining a plant-based shift (Section 4): Risk of abstract, performative answers ('I'd just need to want to do it'). Need to push for specificity about what would actually need to change in concrete daily life — meals, social situations, identity. Consensus risk is also high here: participants may converge on cost or taste as the only barriers.

Social acceptability and gendered meanings of plant-based food (Sections 3 and 5 overlap): Participants may give socially acceptable 'it doesn't bother me' answers about gender and food while simultaneously describing behaviours that contradict this. Logging contradictions early will be important for later reflection probes.

Social context of male friendship and food (Sections 1 and 2 feeding into 3 and 4): The opening sections are opportunities to establish behavioural anchors — specific places, specific meals, specific social situations — that can be referred back to when the discussion moves into more loaded territory around gender and plant-based eating.

participant_notes.anticipated_role: No distinctive profile signals beyond age (45) and suburban South East location. Will watch for whether he engages readily or holds back in early sections before the topics become more loaded.

Oldest participant at 48, East of England suburban. May bring a slightly different regional or generational register. No strong anticipation either way — will monitor for dominance or reticence as session develops.

45, South West suburban. Similar profile to Andrew. Will watch for whether South West location produces any distinctive framing around food culture, pubs, outdoor/rural lifestyle that could be useful behavioural anchors.

Youngest at 40, North West suburban. Generational and regional difference from others may be worth drawing on if the group converges — his experience of food culture in the North West may differ. Will monitor.

47, South East suburban — same region as Andrew. Risk of the two South East participants forming a subtle in-group alignment. Will monitor for this and ensure other voices are drawn in during main topic sections.
participant_notes.initial_attention_flag: Same region as Andrew — watch for alignment or echo dynamic in later sections.

known_risk_conditions: Social desirability on gender: Participants may feel that admitting gender shapes their food choices implies sexism or irrationality. Use behavioural grounding ('think of a specific meal or situation') rather than abstract attitude questions to get around this.

Premature consensus on plant-based barriers: Cost and taste are culturally available, low-risk answers. The group may converge on these quickly without surfacing identity, social, or relational barriers. Plan a sharpening move or invite_dissent if this happens in Sections 4 or 5.

Topic sensitivity around masculinity: Some participants may find explicit discussion of masculinity and food uncomfortable or slightly absurd. The framing should remain grounded in real behaviour and experience, not abstract gender theory.

All participants are suburban men of similar age (40–48): Risk of high group homogeneity producing rapid consensus. Need to actively look for differences in region, context, or specific experience to surface genuine diversity of views.

45-minute session is tight across 6 sections: Intro and closing must be kept brief. Context sections (1–2) serve primarily to warm up and generate behavioural anchors — move to main topics before they exhaust themselves.
initial_session_plan.directivity_plan: Sections 0–1 (intro and male friendship): Light touch. Let participants warm up. Minimal probing. The goal is comfort and concrete anchors, not deep data. Section 2 (everyday food decisions): Moderate directivity. Begin grounding in specific behaviours — what they actually eat, when, with whom. This sets up Section 3. Section 3 (gender and food): Higher directivity. This is the first main topic and social desirability risk is highest here. Use behavioural grounding probes early. Be ready to surface contradictions and invite dissent. Sections 4–5 (plant-based shift and appeal): Highest directivity. These carry the most direct research value. Push for specificity, probe vague or performative answers, watch consensus risk carefully, and use sharpening moves if needed. Section 6 (closing): Light touch. One open invitation, then wrap.

time_budget.budget_rationale: Main topic sections (3, 4, 5) receive the largest share — approximately 55% of total budget between them, weighted toward Sections 4 and 5 which carry the most direct research value. Context sections (1, 2) receive a moderate share — enough to warm up and establish behavioural anchors but not to exhaust the topic. Intro and closing receive minimal allocations. Section 3 receives more than Sections 1–2 because it is the first place where social desirability risk is high and behavioural grounding probes are needed.

per_section.section_label: Opening discussion: male friendship and place

discussion_guide.scripted_question:
Hi everyone, thanks so much for joining the focus group today. We’re
going to take about 45 minutes to talk about your food choices and
opinions, and this will be recorded for research purposes. Try not to
overthink the questions, and simply speak freely. There are no right
or wrong answers. Please be respectful of your fellow focus group
members, and keep your responses relatively brief to allow time for
everyone to speak. But remember that this is a conversation, not an
interview, so you can jump in when you have something to say and you
don’t have to take turns answering each question, but you can if you
want to. Okay great, let’s start by going around and saying your name
and where in the UK you’re coming from today.

discussion_guide.section_label: Opening discussion: male friendship and place
discussion_guide.section_purpose: Section 1: Opening discussion: male friendship and place
discussion_guide.scripted_question:
What’s your favourite place in your city to spend time with your male
friends? Why? Feel free to be specific.
How do you decide what to eat?
suggested_probes: Do other people influence what you eat? If so, tell us more about how.
Do your work or hobbies influence what foods you eat? Tell us more about how.
How important is health and nutrition?

discussion_guide.scripted_question:
Do you think your gender influences what you eat? Tell us more about
why or why not.
suggested_probes: Is it socially acceptable for men to eat vegetarian or vegan foods?

discussion_guide.scripted_question:
Imagine you decided to go plant-based — what would need to change in
your life for you to do that?
suggested_probes: How would your family and friends react to this?
How might it change the way you shop or cook?

discussion_guide.section_purpose: Section 5: Making plant-based foods more appealing
discussion_guide.scripted_question:
What might make plant-based foods more appealing to you or other men
you know?

Okay everyone, that’s our time. Thanks so much for participating
today. Before we finish, is there anything else you would like to add
about food choices, gender, masculinity, or plant-based eating?

group_has_agreed_easily_on: Garages, driveways, and practical activity spaces are preferred male social spaces over pubs for several participants — doing something versus just sitting talking.

last_engagement_round.hook: The realization about the curry text is hitting me—that exact thing. I do that. And it's not just about the meal, it's that I'm making a unilateral decision in the moment without thinking about what she's already planned or bought for. There's something about naming that specific action—texting about a takeaway—that feels like it needs acknowledging, because it's such a small thing that adds up. And I haven't really sat with how that lands for her.

Andrew just recognized the pattern with food decisions the same way he did with household planning — he's seeing how his wife carries the mental load while he opts out. He's at a moment of clarity. I should reinforce this but also name something he hasn't quite said yet: the difference between 'she sorted it out' and actually being responsible for knowing what's needed. That distinction matters because it's where the shift actually happens.

Andrew's just said something that's hitting me — about the food thing, about how he's not thinking about the planning side of it. And I recognize that pattern in myself with food. But there's something he's touched on that I haven't really admitted yet — it's not just that I'm tired or busy. It's that I've kind of opted out because it feels easier, and I'm trying to convince myself that's just who I am. But hearing him say it out loud, about the curry, about texting to say he's grabbing something — that's making me realize I do the exact same thing. And maybe I should actually say that, because it's different from the household stuff we've been talking about. Food is more immediate, more daily. And if I can't even think ahead about that, what does that say about the bigger picture?

Andrew's just realized something about the food/meal planning — how he's opted out of that thinking while his wife carries it. That's hitting close to home for me because I've done exactly the same thing, telling myself it's just how things are because I'm out all day. But what he's saying about not thinking about the ripple effect on her planning — that's something I need to actually own, not just nod along to.

Andrew's just articulated something I recognize in myself — the moment where you realize you've been choosing the easier option and calling it a character trait. He's at that threshold. Also, the food thing is hitting differently because it's concrete and immediate in a way the abstract planning talk isn't. I want to push on what that means for actually changing it.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section centred on how domestic labour and household management are divided between partners, with a recurring tension between flexibility and structure. Work-from-home status emerged as a false proxy for equal sharing — physical presence doesn't resolve mental load. The arrival of children was the sharpest dividing line: those without experienced loose, negotiated arrangements, while those with young or school-age children described non-negotiable fixed rhythms that forced explicit conversations about responsibility.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The opening introductions gave way quickly to an organic Paul–Nick exchange I allowed to run, which usefully surfaced the WFH versus on-the-road contrast early. I intervened to draw in the quieter participants, which worked — Daniel added meaningful depth on mental load and the limits of WFH as a solution. Andrew and John remained unheard throughout, which I acknowledged in my transition prompt. Moving to a lighter, place-based question was a reset aimed at lowering the register and finally opening space for them.

section_summaries.section_label: Opening discussion: male friendship and place
section_summaries.discussion_summary: The section extended the mental load theme from the prior section into new territory: the distinction between doing tasks and carrying anticipatory responsibility sharpened into a challenge about agency. Daniel's direct pushback on John prompted genuine self-reflection from both John and Andrew — acknowledging that long hours are rationalisation rather than obstacle. The garage and physical projects emerged as a comfortable retreat that insulates men from household cognitive labour, with Nick naming this explicitly as a fairness issue.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The place question was a deliberate register-lowering pivot to draw in Andrew and John, and it worked — Andrew answered warmly then voluntarily reconnected to the mental load thread, and Nick followed. The organic return to earlier themes without prompting was a good sign the topic had genuine traction. I made two relatively quick transitions rather than deepening either thread, which kept momentum but may have left the garage-as-refuge insight underexplored. That tension between doing and carrying feels worth revisiting.

transcript.content: Hi everyone, great to have you all here — thanks so much for giving up your time today. We're going to spend about 45 minutes together just having a conversation, and it'll be recorded for research purposes, so I hope that's all fine. My job is really just to keep things moving — this is your conversation, not mine, so I'll mostly be listening. There are genuinely no right or wrong answers to anything we discuss today, and there's no position I'm hoping you'll land on. What I'm interested in is what you actually think and do in real life — the specific, concrete stuff — rather than what might sound like the sensible or correct thing to say. So if something someone else says connects with your experience, or if you see it differently, just jump in — you don't need to wait to be asked. The only thing I'd ask is that you're respectful of each other, and try not to talk over one another too much so everyone gets a chance to be heard. Okay, let's just get started — if we could go around and each say your name and where in the UK you're coming from today, that'd be brilliant.

Right, I'm Paul. I'm from the South East, suburban area, so nothing particularly exotic. Been here a while with my wife. Work from home mostly, which I think has probably shaped how I see things these days.

I'm Nick, I'm from the North West, suburban as well — so yeah, bit of common ground there with Paul. Though work from home though, that's different for me. I'm out on the road most days, moving between jobs, so I don't really get that option. But I know what you mean about it shaping things. My wife's the one doing that side of things now more, and it's changed how we've had to manage stuff at home, especially with the little one. So I'm interested to hear how that's worked out for you, Paul, because our situations are probably quite different but the household side of things... that's been a shift for us too.

Yeah, I mean it's interesting you say that because I think it probably does work differently for us. I'm here, so I can at least keep an eye on things during the day, you know — pop the kettle on, sort a few bits around the house if needed. But I wouldn't say that's meant my wife's picked up less, if I'm honest. It's more that we've both had to be a bit more flexible about it.

Like, she still does most of the shopping, most of the planning. I just... I've got the time to do some of the day-to-day stuff that maybe I wouldn't have done if I was commuting. But it's not like she's stepped back from any of it, really. If anything we've probably just divvied it up a bit more, week to week, depending on what's going on.

I think the thing is, though — and maybe this is where it differs from your situation with the little one — we haven't got kids at home, so there's less of that structured stuff you've got to manage. No school runs or anything like that. That probably makes it easier for us to just... get on with it without it becoming this big issue.

Yeah, the school runs thing is... it's a headache, to be honest. I mean, my wife's managing most of it at the moment because I'm out on jobs, but it's not straightforward. She's trying to get our little one sorted in the morning, get herself ready, and then I'm already out the door heading to whatever site I'm on. So if anything goes wrong — appointment gets moved, school's closed, whatever — it lands on her to sort it, because I can't just nip back or rearrange. I'm committed to being somewhere.

And then there's the planning side of it that you mentioned, Paul. The shopping, the meal planning, all that. My wife does end up carrying a lot of that, yeah. It's not that I'm not helping, but there's a difference between being able to pop something on the shopping list because you're home and thinking about what needs doing, versus me being out all day and... I don't know, it just doesn't work the same way. By the time I'm home in the evening, things are already sorted or they're not, and the decisions have kind of been made.

I think what you're saying about it not being a big issue is probably different for us, because with the young one there's less flexibility. The school run happens at a set time whether you like it or not.

That's a really good point about the fixed rhythms with young kids — sounds like something a few of you might have experience of. We should hear from the rest of you too — Andrew, Daniel, John — over to you.

Yeah, right, I mean — I've got teenagers now, so they're past all that, but I recognize exactly what you're saying, Nick. We went through all that. The thing is, with us, my wife was always the one working full-time — still is — and I've been more... flexible, I suppose. Done the school runs for years, sorted the planning, all that day-to-day stuff. And I'm not going to pretend I was some kind of saint about it, but it just became how we had to manage it because of the work I do, moving around different sites.

But the reason I wanted to push in here is — and I don't mean this at Paul, it's just different situations — but saying it hasn't become a big issue, I think that's only because you haven't got kids depending on fixed times. With us it absolutely became a big issue. It wasn't something we just drifted into. We had to actively sit down and say right, how are we actually going to make this work, because one of us had to be available for the school run, someone had to think about tea, someone had to know where the PE kit was. And it fell to me more often than not, especially in the early years.

It's not a massive problem now they're older, they can sort themselves more. But I wouldn't want anyone to think that just because you work from home you've somehow solved it, or that it sorts itself out. We had to actually decide how to handle it.

No, you're right. I mean, I wasn't trying to suggest we've got it all figured out or that it's effortless or anything like that. I just meant — for us, without kids, there isn't that fixed point in the day where something has to happen, you know? The school run, the PE kit, all that. We don't have that pressure.

But you're fair to call that out. I was comparing it to your situation and sort of brushing past the fact that we're in quite different circumstances. We've still had to work out who does what, and my wife's still planning most of the household side of things. It's just that we've got more room to shuffle things around because nothing's time-dependent. That's a privilege, really, isn't it? Not having that structure forcing your hand.

What you're describing with having to actively sit down and decide how it's going to work — that sounds like something we should've done more deliberately too, probably. Instead we've just kind of muddled through and assumed it was fine.

Yeah, well that's the thing though — it's easy to muddle through if nothing's forcing you to have the conversation. But then you wake up five, ten years down the line and you realize one person's been carrying it all, and you haven't actually talked about whether that's fair or how it got that way.

With us, the conversation happened because it had to. I'd be on a job site thirty miles away and my wife would ring me because the school had rung her about something, and she'd be trying to sort it while she was meant to be at work herself. So we didn't have a choice — we had to actually say, right, this isn't working. And then you've got to figure out what you're going to do about it.

But even then, I think once you've settled into a pattern, it's harder to shift than you'd think. I did the runs, the planning, whatever — but my wife never really stepped back from it mentally, you know? She was still thinking about it, still checking in, still knowing what needed doing. I was doing the physical doing, but she was still carrying the mental load of it. And you don't necessarily realize that's happening until you've been doing it for years and someone points it out or you just notice it.

I'm not saying we've got it perfect now — we don't. But at least we've had the conversation about what's actually happening and why, rather than just assuming it sorted itself out because I happened to be more flexible with work.

Really interesting stuff — that gap between doing and carrying it mentally is something worth sitting with. We should move on though, because I want to make sure Andrew and John get in too. So let's shift to something a bit different — thinking about where you actually spend time with your male friends. What's your favourite spot in your city or town for that? Could be a pub, a park, a mate's house, whatever — somewhere specific.

Yeah, look — what Daniel's saying there about the mental load, that's... that rings true, actually. I've seen that with my wife, or not my wife, but the woman I'm living with. Not quite the same setup as Daniel's got, but similar enough.

She does all the thinking about what needs buying, what needs doing round the house, whether the boiler needs servicing, that sort of thing. And I'm not saying I don't help — I do bits and pieces, maintenance on the van, tinkering in the driveway, that's my domain. But she's the one who's got it all in her head, isn't she? The list of what needs doing. I might fix something when it breaks, but she's the one who noticed it was going to break in the first place.

And that's the difference, innit. The doing versus the carrying it. I can help with the doing, but I'm not... I'm not in that mindset of always thinking ahead about what's needed next. She is. That's just how it's settled, I suppose. With the hours I do, and her being around more, it's kind of fallen that way. But yeah, what you're describing — that mental side of it — that's spot on. That's the bit that doesn't shift even when someone's lending a hand with the physical stuff.

Right, but — and I don't mean this harshly, John — but saying that's just how it's settled, that's where you can get stuck, isn't it? Because it doesn't have to stay that way just because the hours are what they are.

I mean, I work the same kind of hours you do, out on site all day, moving between jobs. But I made myself start thinking about that stuff. Not because I suddenly became naturally good at it or because I had more time — I didn't. But because once I realized that's what was happening, I thought, well, I can actually change this. It's not like it's written in stone.

What I mean is — yeah, my wife knew where the boiler was going to go wrong before I did. But then I started actually asking her what was coming up, what needed looking at. Or I'd notice something needed doing and actually sort it rather than waiting for her to tell me it was broken. And that takes more than just doing the odd job, it takes actually thinking about the household and what's coming down the line.

It's harder work than just doing bits when you're asked, to be honest. But the point is, it's not inevitable. You can shift it if you decide to. It takes a bit more effort on your part, but it's not something that's just locked in because of work patterns. That's the trap — accepting it as just how it settled.

Yeah, fair point. I mean... you're right, I was just saying that's how it's settled like it's not something I could do anything about. But it is, isn't it? I could actually think about it more.

The thing is, with the hours I do — I'm out early, back late most days — it's easy to just... not be in that headspace. You're thinking about the next delivery, the traffic, whether you're going to make the window. And by the time you're home you're knackered. But that's probably just an excuse, really. Because you could still ask what's coming up, what needs sorting. Like you said.

I haven't really done that, to be honest. I just kind of... go along with how things are. She mentions something needs doing, I do it or I don't. But I'm not actually thinking ahead about it, planning what might be needed next month or whenever. I don't know if I'm that type of person, but maybe that's just what I tell myself because it's easier that way.

I suppose it's different from what you're describing — you made yourself get into it. I haven't really tried. So I can't really say it's just impossible because I work long hours, because you work long hours too and you've managed to shift it.

I want to pick that thread back up later because it's relevant to where we're going — but let me actually ask you all the question I meant to start with. What's your favourite place in your city or town to spend time with your male friends? Can be a pub, a park, someone's garage, wherever — what comes to mind, and why that place?

Right, yeah — the lads, that's easy for me. There's a pub down near the high street, the Red Lion, been going there for years now. Nothing fancy about it, just... it's where everyone ends up really. You can sit outside if the weather's alright, grab a pint, talk about whatever — work, football, someone's just done their garden up, that sort of thing. Doesn't have to be anything planned, just a few of us might text and say we're heading down there on a Friday after work or Saturday afternoon.

Though to be honest, as much as anywhere, it's just people's garages and driveways. Someone's working on their car, someone's got a project on, you just pitch up, have a look at what they're doing, grab a tool if needed, sit about. That's probably where I'm most comfortable, if I'm being honest. Less pressure than a pub in some ways — you're doing something, not just sitting talking.

But listen — I was hearing what you two were saying about the household stuff, the planning side of it, and...

Yeah, I recognize that. In my place, that's all my wife as well. The boiler, the bills, knowing when something's going to need sorting — that's all her territory really. I've got the garage, the van maintenance, maybe a bit of the garden, but the house side of things? I'm not... I'm not in that loop the way she is. And hearing John just now saying maybe that's just an excuse, that you could actually try to shift it — that's making me think a bit, because I haven't really questioned it either, have I? It's just how it's always been.

Yeah, I hear what you're saying, Andrew. The garage thing — I get that. I'm the same way, if I'm honest. I've got my projects, my tools, the wiring stuff around the house, the audio equipment I tinker with. That's where I feel like I know what I'm doing, you know? There's a right way to do it, you can see if it's worked or not. It makes sense.

But what Daniel's saying — and what you're picking up on now — that's the thing, isn't it. Because it's comfortable in the garage, you can kind of... stay there. You're doing something, you're being useful, but you're not in the mental load of the household. And it's easy to tell yourself that's just your domain, that's what you're good at, whereas all that planning and thinking ahead, that's just not you.

But I think what Daniel's getting at — and I reckon he's right — is that's not actually true. It's not that you can't do it, it's that you haven't made yourself uncomfortable enough to try. Because it is uncomfortable at first, isn't it? You're not in your comfort zone. You're having to think about stuff that doesn't come naturally, ask questions you should probably already know the answer to, get your head round what's actually coming down the line in the house.

I do a bit of that now because I have to — with the little one, school stuff coming up, the mortgage side of things — but I could probably do a lot more if I actually sat down and... I don't know, asked what's coming up, what's worrying my wife, what she's thinking about that I'm not. Because she definitely is thinking about it. And me staying comfortable in my little projects corner while she's carrying all that, that's not really fair, is it?

There's something interesting in that — the doing something versus just being there thing keeps coming up. Let's carry that with us, actually, because it connects to where I want to go next. I want to shift to something a bit more everyday — food. How do you decide what to eat? Whether that's what you're buying, what you're cooking, what you're ordering — what actually drives those decisions for you?

Yeah, that's... that's a good question, actually.

For me it's pretty much just whatever's quickest or what I fancy in that moment, to be honest. If I'm home late — which is most days — I'm either grabbing something on the way back, picking up a takeaway, or just... there's usually something in the fridge that my wife's sorted out. I don't really think about it much. I just eat what's there or what I feel like having.

But hearing what you've just said, Nick — about your wife thinking about it, planning it — that's the thing, isn't it? I haven't really thought about how much of that sits with her. Like, she's the one who knows what needs buying, what works for the week, whether we've got the right stuff in. And I just show up and eat it, or I text her saying I'm grabbing a curry on the way home because that's what I fancy right then.

She probably has to think about that — like, if I'm not eating at home, she's got to adjust what she's planned. Or she's thinking about whether we've got enough for the week, what we've got coming up. And I'm just... deciding based on what I want in that moment, really. Not thinking about any of the planning side of it.

That's another one where I've just accepted it as, oh well, she's the food person, she handles all that. But it's not that she's the food person, is it? It's that she's the one carrying all the thinking about it, and I'm just... opting out of that side and doing what feels easy. Takeaway or whatever's there.

Yeah, I mean — food's the thing that's made this land a bit differently for me, actually. Because we do talk about it, my wife and I. Or we're supposed to, anyway. Like, she'll ask what I fancy for the week, we'll chat about it, and then... and then she's the one who remembers it all, isn't she? She's the one who's got it in her head.

I might say on a Wednesday I want fish, so she buys fish. But I'm not thinking ahead about Monday, Tuesday, what's coming. She is. And then if I decide halfway through the week I just can't be bothered with what's planned, I'll text and say I'm grabbing something else, and she's the one who's left thinking, well, now I've got this fish sitting here.

What Andrew's just said about that — about not thinking about how that affects her planning — that's hit me a bit. Because I do that too. I tell myself we've got this shared arrangement where we talk about meals, but really what's happening is I get consulted, and then she carries the whole thing. She's thinking about it, adapting when I change my mind, making sure there's something there.

And I haven't really... I haven't made myself do the thinking side of it. I could look at what we've got, think about what's coming in the week, actually plan it out rather than just having an opinion when asked. But that would take more effort than what I'm doing now, which is basically just... saying what sounds good and letting her sort it.
